prompt.context: Our client is a start-up electric vehicle manufacturer that has built a prototype all-electric vehicle and is interested in mass-producing it for the U.S. market. We have been hired to help them think about this opportunity.
prompt.question: How should the client think about mass-producing this electric vehicle for the U.S. market?

clarifying_info.q: What type of vehicle has the client developed?
clarifying_info.a: It is a light-duty all-electric truck. They have manufactured 3 identical prototype vehicles to date.

clarifying_info.q: What are the client's existing manufacturing capabilities?
clarifying_info.a: Minimal. The current manufacturing facility is little more than a large R&D lab.

clarifying_info.q: Where does the client hope to sell their vehicles?
How many vehicles does the client want to produce in Year 1 of manufacturing?
How much will the vehicle retail for?
clarifying_info.a: Pricing has not been determined yet, but will likely be in the $35k-$50k range.

framework: Market sizing and segmentation: identify which customer segments in the U.S. auto market the vehicle targets (luxury, hybrid, SUV/truck class, price tier)
Manufacturing scale-up: determine labor and capacity requirements to hit 150,000 units in Year 1
Manufacturing location options: evaluate build domestic vs. build overseas vs. outsource/JV, with pros/cons of each
Cost reduction strategies within the chosen manufacturing approach
Recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: How would you think about the potential market for this vehicle in the U.S. (i.e. market segments)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should break down different customer segments in the U.S. auto industry: luxury vs. mass-market, hybrid/EV adopters vs. traditional buyers, vehicle class (truck, SUV, sedan), price tier ($35k-$50k positions it mid-to-premium). Candidate should recognize that the addressable market depends on price point, physical characteristics (cargo/passenger space), vehicle range, and distribution availability. A strong answer covers multiple dimensions (price, use case, range needs, buyer psychographics). A weak answer covers only one or two dimensions.

questions.prompt: How many employees will be required to build the desired first-year production run of 150,000 vehicles? The vehicle requires approximately 600 unique assembly steps; each step takes approximately 30 seconds.
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask clarifying questions before calculating: How many hours per day does an employee work? (10 hours/day) How many days per week? (5 days/week = 50 hours/week) How many weeks per year? (50 weeks/year). Then calculate total hours per vehicle and total employee-hours needed.

math.setup: Steps per vehicle = 600; time per step = 30 seconds = 0.5 minutes = 1/120 hour. Hours per vehicle = 600 x (30/3600) = 600/120 = 5 hours per vehicle. Employee hours per year = 10 hours/day x 5 days/week x 50 weeks/year = 2,500 hours per employee per year. Employees needed = (150,000 vehicles x 5 hours/vehicle) / 2,500 hours per employee per year.
steps: Hours per vehicle = 600 steps x 30 seconds/step = 18,000 seconds = 300 minutes = 5 hours
Hours per employee per year = 10 hrs/day x 5 days/wk x 50 wks/yr = 2,500 hours

questions.prompt: What options should the client consider for scaling up manufacturing to mass-produce the vehicle? What are the pros and cons of each option?
questions.guidance: A strong answer is logical, structured, and covers drivers for each option. Three main options: (1) Build a manufacturing facility in the U.S. — pros: proximity to market/suppliers, brand perception, avoids tariffs, regulatory clarity; cons: higher labor costs, higher capex, longer lead time. (2) Build a facility in a low-cost SE Asian country — pros: lower labor costs; cons: shipping costs and time, quality perception risk, regulatory/political risk, distance from suppliers. (3) Outsource production (contract manufacturing or JV) in the U.S. or overseas — pros: lower upfront capex, speed to market, leverage partner expertise; cons: loss of IP control, quality control challenges, dependency on partner. Items to address include labor costs, shipping, quality (actual or perceived), regulation, public reaction, proximity to suppliers. A weak answer covers only one or two areas or fewer than three pros/cons per option.

questions.prompt: Assume the client has decided to build a manufacturing facility in the United States. What are some strategies they could use to reduce costs? Discuss the trade-offs of each approach.
questions.guidance: The core trade-off is automation vs. manual labor: automated technology requires high upfront capital investment and high fixed costs but reduces direct labor (variable) costs; less automation means lower upfront/fixed costs but higher variable costs per unit. Other strategies: (a) Location choice — right-to-work state (lower union costs) vs. union state; (b) Engineering optimization — reduce number of assembly steps (fewer steps = lower labor) vs. vehicle customization options; (c) Supply chain optimization — nearshore suppliers to reduce logistics costs. A weak answer addresses only one cost-savings approach without discussing trade-offs.

questions.prompt: What would you advise the CEO to do regarding the decision to mass-produce an electric vehicle next year?
questions.guidance: There is no single right answer. A strong recommendation is decisive, supported by argument, addresses risks and mitigation, and introduces new insight not already covered. Possible angles: (1) License or sell the technology to an established auto-industry player that has manufacturing and distribution already in place — lower risk, faster path to revenue; (2) Form a JV or strategic alliance with an established player to co-manufacture, sharing capex and risk; (3) Launch a pilot production run (not full 150k) to work out technology kinks and gauge market reaction before full commitment. A weak recommendation merely recaps items from earlier questions without a decisive stance or new insight.

recommendation: Consider licensing or selling the technology to an established auto manufacturer with existing manufacturing infrastructure and distribution, reducing execution risk and time to market
Alternatively, form a JV or strategic alliance with an established player to co-manufacture, sharing capital expenditure and risk while leveraging partner expertise
If the client insists on independent manufacturing, launch a smaller pilot production run first to de-risk the technology and validate market demand before committing to 150,000 units
risks: Manufacturing scale-up from 3 prototype units to 150,000 vehicles in Year 1 is extremely aggressive and operationally risky
Pricing at $35k-$50k competes in a challenging segment against established players; market acceptance is uncertain
Capital requirements for building a U.S. manufacturing facility are substantial for a start-up
Technology risk remains — production vehicles may surface issues not seen in 3 prototypes
next_steps: Conduct market research to validate demand and optimal price point in the $35k-$50k truck segment
Evaluate and approach potential JV partners or licensing candidates among established OEMs
Develop a detailed manufacturing feasibility study and capex model for the U.S. facility option
Define a pilot production milestone (e.g., 1,000 units) to validate production processes before full ramp
